title: Security pillar (protect data and systems)
hook: The Security pillar implements defense in depth: strong identity, least-privilege permissions, encryption everywhere, and continuous detection of misconfigurations and threats.

blocks.text: Principles: implement strong identity foundation, apply security at all layers, automate security best practices, protect data in transit and at rest, keep people away from data, and prepare for security events. AWS services: IAM, Organizations SCPs, KMS, Secrets Manager, Security Hub, GuardDuty, Config, WAF.

entries.plainDefinition: Threat detection from VPC Flow Logs and DNS

entries.example: Lambda role read one secret only

blocks.text: Every architecture review starts with "who can access what?" and "what happens if credentials leak?" Security pillar HRIs — public S3 buckets, overly broad IAM, unencrypted databases — are instant interview red flags.

blocks.title: Interview framing
blocks.body: Say: identity foundation, least privilege, encryption, detective controls, incident response.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Identity foundation
items.body: IAM Identity Center SSO, no long-lived root keys, MFA everywhere.

items.title: Protect data
items.body: Encrypt at rest (KMS) and in transit (TLS). Classify sensitive data.

items.title: Detective controls
items.body: Config rules, Security Hub standards, GuardDuty findings.

items.title: Respond to events
items.body: Runbooks for credential rotation, isolation, forensic snapshot.

diagram.title: Defense in depth
diagram.source:
flowchart TB
  ID[Identity SSO/MFA] --> NET[Network SG/NACL/WAF]

  DATA --> DET[GuardDuty Config]
  DET --> IR[Incident response]

snippet.label: SCP deny public S3
snippet.explanation: Org guardrail prevents accidental public object ACLs.

snippet.label: RDS encryption
snippet.code:
DbInstance:
  Type: AWS::RDS::DBInstance
  Properties:
    StorageEncrypted: true
    KmsKeyId: !Ref DbKey
snippet.explanation: Encrypt at rest — Security pillar baseline for data stores.

snippet.label: Enable GuardDuty
snippet.code:
aws guardduty create-detector --enable
aws guardduty list-findings --detector-id <id> --finding-criteria '{"criterion":{"severity":{"gte":7}}}'

snippet.label: IAM access analyzer
snippet.explanation: Find resources shared externally — common HRI source.

blocks.title: Cloud vs app patterns
rows: KMS at rest + TLS in transit

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Long-lived IAM user access keys in application code. Security groups open to 0.0.0.0/0 on app ports. Ignoring GuardDuty findings as "noise".

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: Security Hub compliance score trend; mean time to remediate Config non-compliance; secrets rotation age; zero public S3 buckets via automated scans.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying "security groups are enough" — rejected. Strong answer: identity + network + data encryption + detective controls + IR.

interviewTakeaways: Security = strong identity, least privilege, encryption, detection, incident response.
Public buckets and broad IAM are top HRIs.
Automate Config rules and Security Hub dashboards for continuous compliance.
60s: SSO/MFA, encrypt data, SCP guardrails, GuardDuty/Config detect issues, runbooks for IR. Defense in depth not one control.
Follow-up: how do SCPs differ from IAM policies?
commonPitfalls: IAM users with access keys in repos — instant rejection.
Strong answer: roles, SSO, Secrets Manager, rotation, no static keys.
Relying only on perimeter SG without data encryption.
Ignoring external access findings from IAM Access Analyzer.

jsTsCorrelations.note: GitHub Actions OIDC replaces long-lived AWS keys — Security pillar best practice.
Never commit secrets; use Secrets Manager SDK with IAM role — same principle as dotenv in dev only.
